summary: Registers the MIME types associated with the 3GPP multimedia file format, which belongs to the family based on the ISO Media File Format. Registration lets software identify and handle these audio and video files on the Internet.

eli5.summary: Phone video files need name tags so computers know what they are. This document makes the official name tags for them.

subtitle: Official media type names for 3GPP phone audio and video files: audio/3gpp and video/3gpp.

tldr.problem: The 3GPP file format holds audio and video for cellular phones, but servers and mail software need registered MIME names to label such files correctly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3839 registers two media types, audio/3gpp for files with audio but no visual material and video/3gpp for any 3GPP file, with the usual file suffix .3gp.
tldr.outcome: Files can be identified over HTTP, in multipart documents and elsewhere MIME types are used. RFC 3839 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6381.

today: RFC 3839 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6381. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The third-generation partnership project (3GPP) for cellular telephony defined a standard file format for audio and visual sequences that may be downloaded to phones. At the time of writing, a 3GP file can contain H.263 or MPEG-4 video, and AMR narrow-band speech, AMR wide-band speech or AAC audio, plus 3GPP timed text.

Like all files in the ISO family, a 3GP file has a file-type box that lists, as four-letter brands, the specifications the file complies with. Files labeled with the MIME types in this RFC MUST list, in their compatible brands, a brand from a 3GPP standard that can apply to 3GPP files.

The types are needed when such files are served over HTTP, included in multi-part documents, or used anywhere else MIME types appear.
sections.eli5: Phone videos are packed in a special kind of box. Each box has a little sticker inside saying which rules it follows. This document gives the box an official name for the outside.

sections.title: Which Files the Registration Covers
sections.content:
The registration applies to all files defined as using the 3GP file format and identified with a suitable brand in a 3GPP specification. The usual file suffix is .3gp.

The published specifications named are 3GPP 26.234, Release 5, and 3GPP 26.244, Release 6 or later. The RFC says the 3GPP organization defines the specification, interoperability and conformance, and runs regular interoperability testing. The change controller is 3GPP.
sections.eli5: Any phone video that follows the 3GPP rules and has the right sticker inside gets one of these names. The usual ending of the file name is .3gp.

sections.title: audio/3gpp and video/3gpp
sections.content:
The type audio/3gpp MAY be used for files containing audio but no visual presentation. Files served under it MUST NOT contain any visual material, and the RFC counts 3GPP timed text as visual because it is displayed.

The type video/3gpp is valid for all files, and it is valid to serve an audio-only file as video/3gpp.

Both registrations have no required parameters and no optional parameters, though the audio registration notes that ongoing work may add an optional parameter to assert the codecs in use without examining the file. Both list the preferred suffix 3gp, also declare 3gpp, and give the Macintosh file type code '3gpp'. Intended usage is COMMON.
sections.eli5: If the box holds only sound, you may label it audio. If it holds pictures or even just words on screen, it must be labeled video. The video label is also fine for any box at all.

sections.title: Encoding and Identifying the Files
sections.content:
Files are binary. They should be transmitted in a suitable encoding without CR/LF conversion or 7-bit stripping, and base64 is a suitable encoding. The RFC stresses these types are used only for files: separate types are used for real-time transfer, such as the RTP payload formats for H.263 and for AMR audio.

There is no magic number in the usual sense. Instead, the file-type box must occur first in the file and MUST contain a 3GPP brand in its compatible brands list.
sections.eli5: These files are not plain text, so they must be sent carefully without changing any bytes. To spot one, look at the very first thing inside the box: the sticker with the brand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The 3GPP format may contain audio, video and displayable text. There is currently no provision for active elements such as scripts. It is possible to author malicious files that call for an excessively large picture size or high sampling-rate audio, but the RFC says clients can and usually do protect themselves.

Some metadata fields may be partly intended to protect the media against unauthorized use or distribution, and the intention is that altering or removing them would be treated as an offense under national agreements based on WIPO treaties. Because the format is extensible, future metadata fields or media formats could in theory induce actions in the recipient, but the referenced specification does not support that. There is no current provision for encryption, signing or authentication of these file formats.
sections.eli5: These files only hold sound, pictures and words, not programs, so they cannot do much harm. A tricky person could make a huge picture to slow a phone down, but phones know how to say no.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's only request to IANA is to register the two media types, audio/3gpp and video/3gpp, as defined in section 3. Each registration is written as a template addressed to ietf-types@iana.org, with the contact given as the Nokia MIME manager.
sections.eli5: The authors ask the official keeper of names to write down the two new names in the big list.

cells: MUST NOT contain any visual material, including timed text
Valid for all files, including audio-only ones
